morphology.summary: An organelle, not a cell: a roughly spherical, membrane-bound sac found in essentially every animal cell, filled with a cocktail of digestive enzymes (acid hydrolases) that work only in its acidic interior. It is the cell's recycling and demolition site - it breaks down material taken in from outside (via phagocytosis/endocytosis) and the cell's own worn-out parts (via autophagy) into reusable building blocks. Discovered by Christian de Duve in the 1950s (Nobel Prize 1974), originally by isolating a membrane-bound particle fraction whose enzymes only became active after the membrane was disrupted - the first clue that the membrane itself was doing protective work.
morphology.kind: single-membrane-bound organelle of eukaryotic cells - part of the endomembrane/vesicular system, built by the Golgi apparatus and trans-Golgi network, not by its own independent genome (unlike the mitochondrion)
morphology.size: Roughly 0.1-1.2 um in diameter in most cells (some tubular lysosomes in phagocytes can extend further); the poster figure uses a representative 0.5 um, at the small end of a typical cell's organelle inventory but present by the hundreds.
morphology.shape: Classically a roughly spherical or oval vesicle, though shape is flexible and lysosomes can be tubular or irregular, especially in actively phagocytic cells like macrophages and neutrophils; primary lysosomes (fresh from the Golgi, few contents) look emptier, while secondary lysosomes / phagolysosomes (actively digesting) look denser and more heterogeneous.
morphology.limiting_membrane: A SINGLE phospholipid bilayer - this is the single most important anatomical fact to get right, and the one this organelle is most often drawn wrong: unlike the nucleus and mitochondrion, which are bounded by a double membrane (two bilayers with a gap between them), the lysosome has only one boundary membrane. Draw it as ONE unbroken line, never a double line, never with a gap or second concentric membrane.
morphology.lumen: The single-membrane-enclosed interior, maintained strongly ACIDIC at approximately pH 4.5-5, roughly a hundredfold higher H+ concentration than the near-neutral (~pH 7.2) cytosol outside. This acidity is not incidental - it is required for the enzymes inside to work, and it is also a safety mechanism (see do-not-draw notes): the lysosome's own enzymes are useless outside it.
morphology.acid_hydrolases: More than 50-60 distinct hydrolytic enzymes (proteases, nucleases, glycosidases, lipases, phospholipases, phosphatases, sulfatases) collectively called acid hydrolases because every one of them is optimally active only at the lysosome's acidic pH and drops off sharply at the neutral pH of the cytosol. They are made in the rough ER, tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi, and delivered to the lysosome by vesicle traffic from the trans-Golgi network - they are enzymes, not tools; draw them as small dispersed granules/particles in the lumen, never as literal scissors, knives or other tool shapes.
morphology.v_atpase_proton_pumps: Vacuolar-type H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) complexes embedded in the limiting membrane are what actively pump protons (H+) INTO the lysosome from the cytosol, at the cost of ATP hydrolysis, building and maintaining the acidic lumen against a roughly hundred-fold concentration gradient. Structurally a V-ATPase has a cytosolic, ATP-hydrolysing V1 head sector sitting on a membrane-embedded V0 proton-pore sector, connected by a central stalk - a lollipop/mushroom shape broadly similar in silhouette to the well-known F1F0 ATP synthase of mitochondria, but running in the OPPOSITE direction (using ATP to pump protons IN, rather than letting protons flow to make ATP) and NOT making ATP itself. Draw a handful of these small stalked particles studding the inside face of the limiting membrane, each with its head/stalk pointing into the lumen.
morphology.glycocalyx: The inner (luminal) face of the limiting membrane is coated with a dense layer of heavily N-glycosylated membrane proteins (chiefly LAMP-1 and LAMP-2, the lysosome-associated membrane proteins) forming a fuzzy protective sugar coat roughly 5-12 nm thick, called the lysosomal glycocalyx. This coat physically shields the membrane's own lipid bilayer from the surrounding acid hydrolases and acidic pH - a nice, often-omitted detail that explains why the lysosome does not simply digest itself from the inside out. Draw it as a fine fuzzy/beaded lining just inside the limiting membrane, distinct from the free-floating hydrolase granules further out in the lumen.
morphology.contents_and_heterogeneity: A REALISTIC lysosome interior is heterogeneous and granular, not a uniform empty bubble: a mix of free acid-hydrolase granules, partly digested material of varying density (protein/lipid/membrane fragments in various stages of breakdown), and, in an actively digesting phagolysosome, recognisable fragments of whatever was engulfed. Electron micrographs of lysosomes read as irregular, moderately electron-dense (grey-to-dark), textured/granular bodies - never a smooth, empty, uniformly pale sac.
morphology.phagolysosome_fusion: The strongest, most teaching-relevant composition for this organelle: a lysosome FUSING with a phagosome (the membrane-bound vacuole formed when a cell engulfs a particle) that contains an engulfed bacterium. This fusion event - forming a phagolysosome - is literally the step that finishes off a swallowed microbe in a macrophage or neutrophil: the phagosome alone is just a membrane bag holding a live bacterium; only after it fuses with one or more lysosomes does it become acidic and receive the acid hydrolases that actually kill and digest the microbe. Draw two separate membrane-bound compartments (a rounder lysosome, denser/more heterogeneous inside, and a phagosome with a visible rod- or coccus-shaped bacterium inside it) shown at the moment their membranes are merging into one, with hydrolase granules and V-ATPase pumps starting to mix into the newly joined compartment.
morphology.colour_note: A lysosome has no colour in life; TEM images are greyscale (a moderately electron-dense granular body). All colour in a teaching illustration is a convention chosen to make the membrane / acidic lumen / hydrolases / V-ATPase / glycocalyx relationship legible at a glance.

structures.note: ONE unbroken phospholipid bilayer - the key anatomical contrast with the double-membraned nucleus and mitochondrion elsewhere in this atlas. Never draw it as a double line.
The enclosed interior, held about a hundred times more acidic than the cytosol. Fill it with heterogeneous granular content, never a uniform empty bubble.
Dozens of distinct enzyme types, active only at the lysosome's acidic pH. Draw as small dispersed granules/particles in the lumen - never as literal scissors, knives or other tool shapes.

Stalked lollipop-shaped pump complexes studding the limiting membrane, using ATP to pump H+ INTO the lumen - the thing that actually keeps the interior acidic. Similar silhouette to mitochondrial ATP synthase but runs in the opposite direction and does not make ATP.

A fine, fuzzy, heavily sugar-coated protein lining on the INSIDE face of the limiting membrane that protects the membrane's own lipids from the surrounding acid hydrolases. A nice detail most illustrations omit - keep it visually distinct from the free hydrolase granules.
Mixed-density fragments of material being broken down, giving the lumen a realistic textured, granular look rather than a smooth empty interior.
The separate membrane-bound compartment holding the engulfed bacterium, shown at the moment its membrane merges with the lysosome's to form a phagolysosome.
A simple rod- or coccus-shaped bacterium sitting inside the phagosome, about to be exposed to the lysosome's acid hydrolases once fusion completes.

do_not_draw: Do NOT draw a double membrane (two concentric bilayers with a gap). That is the nucleus or the mitochondrion - the lysosome has exactly ONE limiting membrane, and getting this right is the whole anatomical point of this poster.

Do NOT draw cristae (deep membrane folds). That is the mitochondrion's inner membrane - the lysosome's limiting membrane is a single, essentially smooth boundary (aside from the small stalked V-ATPase pumps studding it).
Do NOT stud the outside of the membrane with ribosomes. Ribosome-studded membrane is rough endoplasmic reticulum, a different organelle - the lysosome's membrane is smooth on its cytosolic face.
Do NOT draw a stack of flattened membrane discs/cisternae. That is the Golgi apparatus, a separate subject in this atlas - the lysosome is a single rounded vesicle, not a stack.
Do NOT draw a nucleus, nuclear envelope, nuclear pores or chromatin inside it. The lysosome is not a miniature cell.
Do NOT draw the acid hydrolases as literal scissors, knives, saws or other tool shapes. They are enzyme molecules - draw them as small granules/particles, not tools.

Do NOT draw a uniformly empty, smooth, pale interior. A real lysosome (especially an actively digesting one) is heterogeneous and granular inside, with visible partly digested material - an empty bubble is not realistic.

Do NOT anthropomorphise it in the textbook/sem/3d/watercolor styles: no face, eyes or limbs there (a friendly face belongs only on the separate coloring-book page). No text, letters, numbers, scale bars, arrows-with-labels or watermarks baked into any image.

colour_legend.limiting_membrane: #3A7CA5 (steady mid-blue), drawn as a single thin smooth line - deliberately the ONLY membrane line in the whole picture, to make the single-membrane point visually obvious
colour_legend.lumen: #C9A66B (warm amber-tan), the acidic fluid filling the enclosed interior - a warm tone chosen to read as 'acidic/active' in contrast to the mitochondrion's cooler cream matrix
colour_legend.acid_hydrolases: #B5495B (dusty rose-red) small granules dispersed through the lumen
colour_legend.v_atpase: #4E8B72 (soft teal-green) tiny stalked lollipop knobs studding the inside of the limiting membrane, matrix-facing/lumen-facing side
colour_legend.glycocalyx: #E8C86B (pale gold), a fine fuzzy lining directly on the inside of the limiting membrane, distinct from the free hydrolase granules further into the lumen
colour_legend.digested_content: #8B7355 (muted grey-brown) irregular chunks/fragments mixed through the lumen for heterogeneous texture
colour_legend.phagosome: #8FB6D9 (pale sky-blue), a second, separate compartment membrane, lighter than the lysosome's own membrane so the two are easy to tell apart before/during fusion
colour_legend.engulfed_bacterium: #7A9A6B (muted olive-green), a simple rod shape inside the phagosome
colour_legend.note: The lysosome has no colour in life and TEM is greyscale; every colour here is teaching convention. The palette's job is to make the single-membrane / acidic-granular-lumen / V-ATPase-pumps / protective-glycocalyx relationship legible at a glance, and to make the phagosome-fusion story (lysosome + bacterium-containing phagosome merging) read clearly as two compartments becoming one.

sources.title: "Lysosomes" - The Cell: A Molecular Approach, Cooper (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9953)
sources.note: Acid hydrolases active at acidic lumenal pH (~5) but not at cytosolic pH (~7.2); this is a protective double-safety mechanism - even a ruptured lysosome releases inactive enzymes into the neutral cytosol. Proton pump in the lysosomal membrane actively concentrates H+ using ATP, maintaining roughly a hundredfold higher H+ concentration inside.

sources.title: "Transport from the Trans Golgi Network to Lysosomes" - Molecular Biology of the Cell, Alberts et al. (NCBI Bookshelf NBK26844)
sources.note: Lysosomes contain about 40-60 types of hydrolytic enzymes (proteases, nucleases, glycosidases, lipases, phospholipases, phosphatases, sulfatases), all acid hydrolases, optimally active around lumenal pH 5.0; an H+ pump (V-ATPase) in the membrane uses ATP hydrolysis to acidify the lumen; the same/similar V-ATPase acidifies endosomes and other endocytic/exocytic organelles.

sources.title: "The Acid Gate in the Lysosome" (Autophagy journal / Taylor & Francis)
sources.note: V-ATPase structure: cytosolic ATP-hydrolysing V1 sector on a membrane-embedded V0 proton-pore sector; rotary mechanism transfers protons across the membrane per ATP hydrolysed; maintains the ~pH 4.5-5.0 optimum for hydrolases and autophagy.

sources.title: "Lysosomal membrane glycoproteins bind cholesterol and contribute to lysosomal cholesterol export" (eLife)
sources.note: LAMP-1/LAMP-2 are the major constituents of the lysosomal glycocalyx, a glycoconjugate coat on the inside of the limiting membrane (~5-12 nm thick by EM) that protects the membrane from the lysosome's own acidic, hydrolase-rich environment; removing their N-linked glycans causes their rapid degradation, underscoring the glycosylation's protective role.

sources.title: "Crystal structure of the conserved domain of the DC lysosomal associated membrane protein: implications for the lysosomal glycocalyx" (BMC Biology / PMC3409847)
sources.note: Structural basis for the LAMP-family glycocalyx model that coats and protects the luminal face of the lysosomal membrane.

sources.title: "Phagolysosome" overview (ScienceDirect Topics, aggregating primary immunology literature)
sources.note: Phagosomes formed by macrophages/neutrophils engulfing bacteria mature via sequential fusion with endosomes and then lysosomes to form the phagolysosome; acidification (to pH <=5.0, driven by V-ATPase) activates the lysosomal hydrolases that kill and digest the ingested microbe - the basis for the phagosome-fusion composition chosen here.

sources.title: Wikipedia - Lysosome
sources.note: General reference: size range ~0.1-1.2 um; discovered by Christian de Duve in the 1950s (Nobel Prize 1974) by observing that isolated lysosomal enzymes were latent until the membrane was disrupted; role in both endocytic/phagocytic digestion and autophagy of the cell's own components.
